articles.title: Former German spy chief arrested for espionage and treason
articles.text:
Former German spy chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, the German Federal Prosecutor's Office says.

Hanning headed the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant.

Prosecutors allege that he used classified intelligence to "draft an analysis" for one foreign intelligence service and maintained contact with another foreign spying service. Investigators have not disclosed which foreign powers were involved.

Police also arrested former BND employee Manfred D, accusing him of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents for money.

Manfred D, who was Hanning's bureau chief and remained in the BND until this year, is charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.

Local media reported Hanning was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near Münster while Manfred D was arrested in Bavaria. Hanning is due in court on Wednesday and Manfred D will appear on Tuesday.

Prosecutors say Manfred D, who also served as the chief of staff for Hanning's successors between 2012 and 2026, used his role to gain access to highly confidential information which he then passed on to Hanning "in exchange for remuneration".

"The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes," the statement says.

"On one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence ... to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service," prosecutors said, noting it was not clear if "the material reached the intended recipient".

Hanning is also accused of being "in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D, for several years".

Local media say Hanning's alleged possession of intelligence documents came to light during a separate case relating to German steakhouse heiress Christina Block.

Hamburg public prosecutor's office accused Block of orchestrating the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Investigators allege Hanning was involved in an earlier attempted kidnapping of the children, which he denies.

State criminal police officers reportedly discovered an electronic data storage device containing sensitive information including recent BND documents.

It is not the first time the BND has faced similar controversy. A high-ranking German intelligence officer was charged with treason in 2023 for allegedly passing state secrets to Russia.

Prosecutors alleged Carsten L shared intelligence about the war in Ukraine and the Wagner mercenary group and received roughly €400,000 ($450,000; £340,000). His trial is ongoing.

articles.title: UK special forces could face prosecution as Afghanistan evidence referred to police
articles.text:
UK special forces (UKSF) personnel could face prosecution after evidence found following enquiries by the SAS Inquiry, suggesting serious offences may have been committed in Afghanistan, was handed to the military police.

The evidence came to light in court proceedings on Monday and is the first time the inquiry has publicly acknowledged that its findings could lead to criminal prosecutions.

The referral - made by UKSF earlier this year - was required under the Armed Forces Act, which defines Schedule 2 serious offences as including murder and manslaughter.

It relates to a number of detention operations carried out by British personnel between 2010 and 2013.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) found the evidence earlier this year, following investigation by the SAS Inquiry, and then UKSF referred it to the military police's Defence Serious Crime Unit (DSCU), a specialist unit set up in 2022 to deal with the most serious crimes.

Court documents obtained by the BBC suggest that the DSCU has undertaken a scoping exercise of the evidence, but the unit has paused any criminal investigations until the inquiry has been concluded.

Separately, the MoD told the BBC it was deemed inappropriate for criminal investigations to be undertaken while the inquiry was still ongoing.

The Independent Inquiry relating to Afghanistan is examining allegations that the British Army's Special Air Service (SAS) unlawfully killed people during detention operations in Afghanistan between 2010 and 2013, and that senior officials sought to cover up the true circumstances of the killings.

BBC Panorama has been investigating allegations the SAS executed handcuffed civilians and children, for more than eight years. The public inquiry was established in 2022 in the wake of Panorama's revelations.

The DSCU referral came to light during a High Court hearing brought by a witness to the inquiry.

The witness, a senior British military officer who served in Afghanistan, has won permission to have the inquiry judicially reviewed after military witnesses' legal teams were excluded from closed-door evidence hearings with whistleblowers.

Much of the public inquiry's evidence is being heard in secret.

Lawyers for the senior officer argued the process was unfair and the officer should have an opportunity to question the whistleblowers, either in person or through his lawyers, regarding any allegations made against him.

The inquiry's lawyers said it "must be able to obtain highly sensitive information" from people who may be concerned about giving evidence.

They said protected witnesses had raised fears of "grievous consequences by UKSF" if their identities were revealed.

Get in touch using SecureDrop, a highly anonymous and secure way of whistleblowing to the BBC which uses the Tor network. Or use the Signal messaging app, an end-to-end encrypted message service designed to protect your data.

articles.title: Childminder who left 27 children alone in her home pleads guilty to neglect
articles.text:
A Dunfermline childminder has admitted leaving more than 20 children she was caring for alone and unsupervised in her home.

Amanda Mathewson, 55, pleaded guilty at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court to neglect and abandoning children in her care.

Her offending took place at a number of locations in Dunfermline and elsewhere in Fife.

The court heard Mathewson had 27 children in her home, 19 more than she was licensed to look after.

Mathewson, who has been a self-employed childminder for 30 years, was arrested by police following allegations of cruelty towards children.

The court heard she had provided childcare services at her home in Dunfermline for children under the age of 16.

At the time of her arrest she had 15 children aged under 12, 10 children under primary school age, and two children under the age of one in her care.

Procurator fiscal Vicki Bell told the court two parents became suspicious of Mathewson after being informed their children were not present while the childminder carried out a school run.

They secretly went to the school and found their children were not with Mathewson, despite being in her care.

They then went to her home, where they heard a "child screaming" and found five unattended children in the garden.

One of the children told the witnesses there were no adults inside, and Mathewson had told them to "wait in the garden".

They approached the door of the house to check if there were any adults present, when they hear another child "screaming hysterically" inside.

The door was unlocked, and when the witnesses entered they found a child crying under the kitchen table.

A further nine children, all under five, were found in an upstairs bedroom. Two of them were strapped into prams. The children were said to be "distressed" but uninjured.

Police attended and Mathewson said the children had been left alone for at least 30 minutes.

The court heard ring doorbell footage showed it was the second time that day the children had been left inside the house.

During the police investigation, various children told their parents that being left alone in Mathewson's home was "commonplace".

Some parents told officers that their children became "upset" when they were taken to the childminder's home and those who could talk would say they did not want to go.

The investigation found discrepancies in the number of children in Matthewson's care and the number of children she was seen with on multiple occasions.

For example, Mathewson attended a church Christmas party with three children, despite having nine kids in her care that day.

The parents of the three children who were in attendance were sent a photo of their child with Santa, while the others were just sent a generic photo.

There were other occasions such as a sports day and a visit to Dunfermline fire station where Mathewson was seen with fewer children than she was responsible for.

Parents also raised concerns that their children had not eaten while in the childminder's care due to their clothes staying in "pristine condition" and it was a general theme that their children would return home thirsty.

Some parents also reported their children returned home in dirty nappies or with dry faeces in their underwear.

Court documents state that Mathewson always had loud music playing and did not let parents enter her home at drop off time in an attempt to "conceal how oversubscribed she was".

When the childminder was asked about the number of children in her care, or the whereabouts of certain children she claimed she was being assisted by a "child-minding friend".

A spokesperson for the Care Inspectorate said it was a "distressing case" and they had implemented changes as a result.

Police Scotland said it was a "complex investigation" that involved working with a number of partner agencies.

A force spokesperson said: "We remain wholly committed to supporting victims of crime and protecting children from harm and will use all available resources during our investigation.

"We urge anyone with concerns about a child protection matter to speak to police, external in the knowledge that you will be fully supported and listened to."

In a statement given to the BBC, one of the parents said: "The criminal case is important for justice. But our ultimate goal is to ensure no other family has to endure what we have been through. Our trust was broken, but our resolve is not.

"We have turned our pain into a purpose: to rebuild the system of childcare regulation and family support so that it is truly fit to protect Scotland's children."

Sheriff John MacRitchie deferred sentencing until 6 November to allow background reports to be carried out. Mathewson's bail was continued.

articles.title: Jeffrey Archer: Queen Camilla pays tribute to 'irrepressible' author and former politician
articles.text:
Queen Camilla has paid tribute to the bestselling author and former politician Jeffrey Archer, who has died at the age of 86.

"Seldom does an author get to live a life as rich, varied and colourful as any of the characters in their books, or with as many surprising plot twists," the Queen said in a statement.

She added that Archer was "not without flaw", but that "friends will recall him as an irrepressible life force through all the many differing chapters of his life".

The former Conservative MP was jailed for perjury in 2001 after being found guilty of lying and cheating in his 1987 libel case against the Daily Star.

The Queen said he was "an exception to the end" and that it was "with sadness that I learned of his death yesterday, on the eve of publication of his final work and so soon after appearing at my Queen's Reading Room Festival".

Archer was a supporter of the Queen's Reading Room charity.

"My sympathies go to Mary and the family at this time of sorrow. I hope it may be some consolation for them to know what pleasure Jeffrey brought to me and to so many millions of readers through the pages of his works.

"Wherever the next page turns to, I trust there will be champagne and Shepherd's Pie in abundance. Camilla R."

Archer's parties were known for serving champagne and shepherd's pie to guests.

Archer sold more than 300 million books in his five-decade writing career, including the Clifton Chronicles and Kane and Abel, and often set the novels in his home town of Wellington, Somerset.

In a statement, Archer's publisher HarperCollins said the author died "suddenly and peacefully at home" on Monday between writing sessions.

Archer was born in north London in 1940 but soon moved to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset and in 1969, Archer was elected MP for the Lincolnshire constituency of Louth.

He served as an MP for five years before becoming Conservative Party deputy chairman.

He moved to the House of Lords in 1992 but was jailed for four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice in 2001.

He was found to have lied in libel action he had brought against the Daily Star newspaper, in which he was awarded £500,000 in damages.

The Star had alleged Archer had slept with a sex worker.

The peer was found by the court to have perverted the course of justice by asking a former friend to give him a false alibi and producing fake diary entries to back up his story.

He was also found to have perjured himself on oath during the libel trial.

He was released from jail in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described Archer's death as "devastating news".

"We will miss him very much," she told BBC Breakfast on Tuesday, adding that he had texted her earlier on Monday.

Badenoch said he was "very much loved by the Conservative family", adding: "I'm glad that I saw him recently."

Speaking about what she described as "other parts of his life", she said: "He did serve his time, he made amends, and he wanted to do a lot of good in the world."

Former Conservative prime minister Sir John Major said "we have lost a man who lived one of the most remarkable lives of our age", and that he will be "much missed – and long remembered".

Archer's last novel, Adam and Eve, was released on Tuesday.

Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth told BBC Breakfast that he was with Archer on Sunday. "I mean, literally 72 hours ago, doing a show in the West End of London celebrating this book, the publication, and he was in great form.

"He didn't really acknowledge that he'd changed much since being in prison, but I think he became a nicer person in some ways, a gentler, a milder person after the prison experience."

Former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith described Archer as "a remarkable man who did everything at full bore", adding: "There were simply no half measures with him."

Other former ministers also paid tribute. Sajid Javid said Archer had been a "dear friend", while Sir Jeremy Hunt said Archer had "showed enormous kindness with his advice about how to become a writer".

James Cleverly said the author and politician had been "a huge personality and fantastic storyteller", and that he had been very supportive when his wife Suzie was recovering from cancer.

Reform UK member and former Conservative minister Nadim Zahawi, wrote: "Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey's company."

Last week, Archer returned to his former school to promote his last book.

"It's wonderful to come back. What I got a real thrill about when I was walking towards the library is seeing the young boys and girls and thinking, 'that's the next generation'," Archer said at Wellington School.

Archer had been due to attend the Cheltenham Literature Festival on Saturday to discuss his final novel.

He and his wife Mary had celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary this year, HarperCollins said.

The couple have two sons and five grandchildren.

articles.title: What is pneumonic plague and how does it spread?
articles.text:
The World Health Organization has asked Russia for more information on the death of a worker at a Siberian plague research laboratory.

It is still not clear exactly what led to the worker falling ill, but media reports have led to a flurry of speculation.

Russian officials are still investigating the cause of the death, but they say those who came into contact with the researcher all tested negative for pneumonic plague.

So what is pneumonic plague, and how dangerous is it?

Pneumonic plague is a really serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.

There are two other types of plague: bubonic, which affects the lymph nodes; and septicaemic, which affects the blood.

Pneumonic plague can occur after an initial infection of one of these other types.

Symptoms include shortness of breath, chest pain, and often coughing up blood.

It's regarded as being more serious but less common than bubonic plague.

The global number of infections of all three types of plague varies each year, but it is probably somewhere between 1,000 to 3,000 cases.

Most of these are bubonic plague, and many of them occur in central Africa, but cases also develop in other places, including Russia, India, China, and the United States.

Prof Piero Olliaro is Professor of Poverty-Related Infectious Diseases at the University of Oxford.

He said: "Plague itself has not disappeared: the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, persists in animal reservoirs across many parts of the world.

"Around 200 rodent species can harbour the bacterium, with reservoirs found across the Americas, Eurasia and Africa.

"Sporadic human cases therefore continue to occur, but established surveillance, infection-control measures and effective antibiotic treatment are important tools for limiting their impact."

Plague is an infectious disease caused by bacteria usually found in small mammals and their fleas.

You can catch it by getting bitten by an infected flea or handling an infected animal.

But human-to-human transmission of pneumonic plague is also possible through coughing infected droplets into the air, which are then breathed in by another person, although this normally requires quite close contact.

You can also develop it if you have had septicaemic plague and the infection then spreads into the lungs.

It's thought that pneumonic plague was the main type of plague behind what is known as the Black Death, the massive outbreak that killed millions of people across Europe in the 14th Century.

Dr Zania Stamataki, Associate Professor of Viral Immunology at the University of Birmingham, says it is important that researchers are able to study diseases like plague.

"I understand why people find the idea of plague in a laboratory alarming, so it is worth saying why that work exists," she said.

"Plague is not a historical disease. It remains endemic in rodent populations across Africa, Asia and the Americas, and human cases occur every year, including outbreaks of the pneumonic form.

"Diagnostics, vaccine development and surveillance for antibiotic resistance all require laboratories that hold and study the live organism.

"This work is vital to prepare against outbreaks."

According to the World Health Organization, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours.

If it isn't diagnosed and then treated quickly, experts warn it is nearly always fatal.

But the good news is that plague responds well to antibiotics if the treatment starts early.

Dr Malick Gibani, Clinical Associate Professor in Bacterial Vaccinology at Imperial College London, says the infection is widely recognised as a serious threat to public health.

"Pneumonic plague is a very severe manifestation of plague disease.

"Some textbooks will say it has 100% mortality if left untreated, and it's difficult to have accurate figures in the modern age.

"It is treatable with antibiotics, particularly if started early.

"That's why anyone with high-risk potential exposure might be offered post-exposure prophylaxis with antibiotics and/or quarantine."

In the Russian case, it is still not yet clear whether the person who died was infected by pneumonic plague.

The authorities in Russia have issued a statement saying that tests had shown "no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities" – and so at this stage it is still not quite clear what has happened.

US President Donald Trump said Washington was looking "very strongly" at the case, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no cause for alarm.

The UK's Health and Safety Authority said it was seeking more information, but that the risk to Britain's population was "very low".

articles.title: Ship sinks and crew missing after Black Sea drone attack
articles.text:
A civilian cargo ship has sunk and its crew is missing after being attacked by drones in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials say.

A second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. Its 18 crew were rescued.

Radev did not say who was behind the attacks, which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine.

Moscow has not commented on the latest incident, a day after it was accused by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of striking a civilian vessel carrying corn. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks were "unacceptable".

Air and sea drones were involved in the attacks at about 03:00 (23:00 GMT), some 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, Radev said.

The sunken ship was flying under the flag of Togo, he said. Named the Alfa Watan, it was a Turkish-owned general cargo ship and was reportedly heading for Sulina, Romania.

It is not clear what the Alfa Watan was carrying or how many people were on board.

A Bulgarian vessel was close by, but when they arrived all they saw was an overturned boat and rafts as well as life jackets. A search operation has been launched.

Radev said Bulgarian sailors had rescued the crew members from the second ship - including two who were injured in a fire on board. Eleven were Turkish and seven Indian nationals. That ship, the Able, was flying the flag of Palau and transporting grain.

Its last reported position was five nautical miles (9km) from the Alfa Watan.

Radev condemned the strikes as "a flagrant violation of maritime law".

He told reporters: "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable."

He did not accuse Russia of carrying out the strikes, but referred to the war in Ukraine, saying: "As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning.

"Commercial ships – and innocent crews – are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea," she said. "While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning."

"Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable."

Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea is just over 29,000 sq km (11,197 sq miles), about 6% of the total size of the Black Sea.

articles.title: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego
articles.text:
Donald Trump's remark that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego has sparked fierce backlash from California politicians - and a strongly worded rebuttal from the White House.

California Governor Gavin Newsom condemned the comment - made by Trump at a campaign rally in Nebraska - as "deranged and dangerous," while LA Mayor Karen Bass described them as threats and an attempt to "encourage attacks on American lives".

According to the White House, however, Trump was saying that American cities would have been threatened by Iran had he not launched a war there earlier this year.

Both LA and San Diego house major US military installations including Navy ports and Air Force bases.

Trump, while speaking on Monday in Nebraska about the Iran conflict, said: "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego."

There were cheers from sections of the audience as the comments about the two Californian cities were made.

The morning after Trump's statement, Governor Newsom announced that the "dangerous - if not treasonous" statement had prompted him to direct California's State Threat Assessment Center to "monitor the situation in the event that foreign actors interpret the remarks as an invitation" to target California.

The agency is designed to detect and prevent security threats in the state.

San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote that the city was not collateral damage in a post on X, while demanding Trump keep it out of his "reckless war talk".

Trump is yet to respond to the statements made by California's leaders.

In a post on X, White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung described the "media freakout" over Trump's comments as "not rooted in reality".

"He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," Cheung wrote. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money".

The president and other administration officials often claim that disrupting Iran's nuclear programme was essential for US national security, and that any issues that have stemmed from the conflict were necessary.

A separate X post, from the official White House rapid response account, described journalists from the Los Angeles Times reporting on the comments as "buffoons" and again pushed back on the characterisation of the comments by Newsom and others.

"He was saying the US is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon — which they would if they had the chance," the account added.

San Diego, located 17 miles (27km) from the border with Mexico, is the eighth largest city in the US and is home to Naval Base San Diego, the home port of the US Navy's Pacific Fleet, and Naval Amphibious Base Coronado - the main training centre Navy Seals on the West Coast.

It is also where Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton is located, a base which 70,000 service members and civilians work at.

Located approximately 120 miles (193 KM) north of San Diego, Los Angeles is the second most populous city in the US.

It is home to the space system command headquarters of the US Space Force, as well as the Los Angeles Air Force Base.

articles.title: Defence lawyer in Cornell University case calls for special prosecutor Letitia James to be removed
articles.text:
A lawyer for one of the seven men accused of participating in a Cornell University gang rape has called for the special prosecutor on the case to recuse herself over past public comments.

The lawyer had said a social media post from New York Attorney General Letitia James throws into question her investigation's "integrity and independence".

In the 28 September post, James wrote that "what this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable" and told survivors that "we stand with you".

The university's administration is under fire over its alleged mishandling of the October 2024 incident and, according to US media, now faces a no-confidence vote by Cornell faculty.

The university's Faculty Senate, a governing body comprised of professors and other academic staff, will vote on a resolution of no confidence next week, according to reports. Cornell is an Ivy League university, alongside Harvard and Yale, and its faculty includes Nobel laureates and other distinguished researchers.

A majority no-confidence vote would be a largely symbolic gesture, signalling the broader faculty's discontent and applying pressure on university leadership to act.

The BBC has reached out to Cornell University for comment.

Allegations made in a lawsuit against seven men and the university have rocked the campus in New York state, with hundreds of students and faculty members gathering there on Monday in protest, and sparked anger across the country.

articles.title: NHS supply lorry drivers to strike in pay dispute
articles.text:
NHS supply lorry drivers are set for a series of strikes in a dispute over pay.

Drivers employed by GXO in Tyne and Wear, Derbyshire, Yorkshire, Kent, Warwickshire and Suffolk will stage five walkouts from October 13-15, 20-22, 27-29 and November 3-5 and 10-12, Unite said.

Union members have rejected a 4% pay offer from GXO, which runs the NHS supply chain contract for Supply Chain Coordination Limited (SCCL), and is wholly owned by NHS England.

Unite regional officer Phil Silkstone said: "There is still time for strike action to be avoided but that will require a deal our members can accept." NHS Supply Chain and GXO said they had "robust contingency plans" in place to minimise disruption.

Drivers deliver general equipment such as bandages, dressings, gowns, gloves and needles to hospitals across England.

Silkstone described them as "dedicated workers" and said GXO had refused to put forward a reasonable offer.

NHS Supply Chain and GXO said they were aware Unite members had voted in favour of industrial action. GXO said it believed the 4% pay offer was fair.

A spokesperson for GXO said: "Patient care remains of paramount importance, and we remain focused on providing a safe and effective operation throughout this period."

Depots where strike action is due to take place are in Alfreton in Derbyshire, Bridgwater in Somerset, Normanton in West Yorkshire, Maidstone in Kent, Rugby in Warwickshire, Bury St Edmonds in Suffolk and Washington in Tyne and Wear.

articles.title: We're saving £100 a month for our kids but they won't get it until they're 57
articles.text:
Richard and Caitlin Brain's two children are aged just 20 months and five months respectively, yet mum and dad have already set up pensions for them.

The Brains, who live in Swansea, south Wales, are paying £50 a month into each of their kids' accounts. It's money that the children won't be able to access until they are 57, under current UK private pension fund rules., external

So the eldest will have to wait until 2082, and the youngest until 2083.

Despite the wait, Richard, 30, is convinced that he and Caitlin, 28, are doing the right thing.

"Paying into their pensions means we can play a part in their future far beyond our own years. And the money has decades to grow."

Richard's financial knowledge is explained by the fact he works for an investment firm. Caitlin is currently on maternity leave from her job working for the local council.

He earns less than £90,000 a year, while she currently doesn't have an income as she has not yet returned to work after her statutory maternity pay of £194 a week ended.

In addition to their children's pensions, Richard and Caitlin have also set up Junior ISA savings accounts for them, and pay in £60 a month per child - money the kids will be able to access when they turn 18.

The couple believe this is the best of both worlds – the ISAs could help their children with university costs, starting a business or a house deposit, while the pensions are intended to provide financial security much later in life.

Paying a combined £220 a month into their kids' funds, in addition to £200 into their own private pensions and savings, the couple say they must live more frugally than in the past.

"We're not on the breadline, but investing this money does mean doing a little less," says Richard. "We don't eat out as often as we used to, which as foodies is a pain.

"And we don't go as big for one another on birthdays and Christmas so that we can still do it for the kids."

Pensions for children, also called Junior self-invested personal pensions (SIPPs), were introduced in the UK in 2001. You can pay in a maximum of £2,880 per year, which the government will then top up with £720 tax relief to make a total £3,600.

The popularity of Junior SIPPs has grown, industry figures show.

One provider, Hargreaves Lansdown, says that in the 12 months to April 2026 it had seen two and a half times as many accounts open, external as in the same period a year earlier.

Another, Fidelity, says it has seen the number of accounts more than triple since December 2023.

While giving their kids a pensions head start is a powerful incentive for some parents, how do the children themselves feel about not being able to touch the money for potentially 50 years or more?

Fifteen-year-old Hugo Thompson from Manchester seems unfazed. His parents, who work in finance, have been paying the maximum amount into his Junior SIPP for the past 10 years.

"The money invested means perhaps I'll be ahead when I'm older," he says. "So I won't have to put quite so much of my own money in! I want to retire earlier than the state pension age so this will all help."

Hugo's mother Annabel, who works in finance, also saves into a Junior ISA for him, but says she still also invests into her own pension and savings. "For me, Junior SIPPs should only be considered once you feel you have enough money of your own," she says.

"My dad passed away when I was very young, and my mom did everything she could to provide for us, often with just the bare minimum," says Wally.

"For much of my adult life, I have felt like I was trying to catch up financially, particularly because of significant student loan debt.

"I don't necessarily think of this as specifically saving for my kids' retirement. I think of it as giving them a head start and helping change the trajectory of our family financially."

articles.title: Lego fraudster among last year's most high-profile insurance scammers
articles.text:
A scammer jailed for making false home insurance claims about supposedly stolen Lego has been listed as one of last year's most high-profile insurance fraudsters.

The person was sentenced to 28 months in prison after an investigation found the claims were made up, insurance trade body the ABI said.

Other insurance fraud cases flagged by the ABI include someone who staged car crashes with people they met online and a complex travel insurance scam involving multiple fake identities and documents.

The average value of a fraudulent claim reached £14,300 last year, the second-highest level on record, the ABI said.

There were £1.34bn worth of fraudulent claims in 2025, a 14% increase on the £1.18bn detected the previous year.

At the same time, the number of detected fraudulent claims fell slightly to 93,900, down 2.7% on 2024.

Mark Allen, head of fraud and financial crime at the ABI, said: "Although the rate of detected insurance fraud fell slightly last year, our data shows that fraudsters are targeting much bigger payouts.

"As emerging technologies such as AI become more widely available, fraudsters will continue to look for new ways to exploit them."

Det Ch Insp Simon Klust, head of the Insurance Fraud Enforcement Department (IFED) at the City of London Police, said: "Insurance fraud is not a victimless crime and those who commit it increase the cost of premiums for honest customers."

He added that the 250 cases a day detected by the ABI last year were "unfortunately likely to be just the tip of the iceberg".

articles.title: What is the future for our medium-sized shopping centres?
articles.text:
The Brunel Centre was once a thriving retail destination, attracting shoppers from far and wide.

"It was incredible," says town councillor Keith Ely, who remembers its opening in Bletchley, Buckinghamshire, in 1973.

Back then, centre:MK, a large destination shopping centre four miles away in Milton Keynes, did not exist, and the Brunel was quite the draw.

Now, like many other medium-sized shopping centres, it is struggling.

Vacant units and graffiti-daubed shutters dominate, and it has just one store left.

That remaining shop, a Boots Opticians, is set to close later this month ahead of the centre's planned demolition next year.

But Ely, 87, is not upset to see the Brunel make way for flats and a health centre, with only some retail space.

"It is a sad old building, isn't it?" he says. "There is no nostalgia from me."

In the Grafton Centre, Cambridge, it is a similar story, with shuttered units, a large empty former Debenhams department store and a permanently closed cinema.

There are long-term plans for a redevelopment to include retail but also a life science centre.

This may work in Cambridge, a global leader in life sciences, but it is not an option in much of the country.

So, in the age of online shopping, what lies ahead for these medium-sized malls?

"There are too many in the UK and many don't have a future," is the stark assessment of Subjit Jassy, a director at Pioneer Group, which owns the centre.

"The old model of retailers expanding to improve turnover has now disappeared because of the internet."

"It is not just that shopping centres have one destiny; they really don't," says Dr Kardi Somerfield, a lecturer in marketing at the University of Northampton.

Some destination shopping centres are running at "almost 100% occupancy", she adds.

Back at the Brunel, Labour's Ed Hume, responsible for housing at Milton Keynes City Council, says: "We do need shops.

"The change here is about making sure we have a town centre that is much more open."

The hope is that more town centre homes will increase the number of people to use local businesses.

Similar plans in Norwich will see the Anglia Square development primarily replaced by housing.

George Grande, voice lead at Silhouette, says being located in a shopping centre means more people can easily arrive by public transport and gives the group more visibility.

"We've had it before where people are like 'Oh, what's this? We don't know what this is.'

"That is how we can get other people to join us."

articles.title: Nifty: Five reasons India's markets are sinking even when its economy is growing
articles.text:
India's economy is growing at an enviable rate of over 7% despite global energy shocks, rising interest rates, tariff uncertainties and weather-related disruptions.

But the world's fastest growing major economy also has one of the worst performing major equity markets in 2026. The correction in Indian stocks has, in fact, only intensified in recent weeks.

The benchmark Sensex and Nifty indices, which represent the country's largest companies, have inched up slightly since Monday after posting losses for eight straight weeks - the longest losing streak in 25 years, according to Reuters.

Indian mom-and-pop investors who put their money into the Nifty have seen their wealth erode by about 15% this year. In comparison, they would have made 62% returns on Korea's Kospi index since January or 170% in the last two years.

On aggregate, the money foreign investors have put into Indian markets in the past decade - after subtracting what they sold or withdrew - is nearing zero. In the past two years alone, foreign institutional investors have withdrawn a staggering $40bn, according to data from Bernstein Research.

It is the large pool of domestic institutional and retail money, flowing into instruments like mutual funds, that have helped the markets avoid a sharper fall.

Domestic assets under management of mutual funds have grown from about $125bn in 2016 to some $900bn this year, with the number of Indians parking money in stocks and mutual funds more than tripling to 150 million individuals.

This makes the recent fall in the markets more worrying - since households, already struggling from a weak job market, high inflation and faltering consumption, are now seeing their equity savings take a beating too.

So, what's gone wrong?

Here are five reasons India's booming economy isn't lifting its stock market.

Crude oil prices have hovered between $90 and $100 a barrel as the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz enters its eighth month, far longer than analysts had expected. Moreover, there's little visibility on when normalcy will return.

"This single variable tends to influence the markets quite negatively," Hari Shyamsunder, a fund manager with Franklin Templeton Asset Management India, told the BBC. "Markets can absorb crude between $70 and $90, but when prices move above $100 a barrel, it starts putting stress on macro-economic variables such as inflation and also company earnings and margins."

India imports over 90% of its requirements - nearly half of its crude oil imports, along with a large share of its liquified petroleum gas (LPG) and liquified natural gas (LNG) shipments, come through the Strait of Hormuz.

While Delhi has diversified its energy sources, tapping Russian oil markets, US President Donald Trump recently threatened up to 100% tariffs on countries doing trade with Moscow, further complicating matters.

articles.title: Pentagon stops using Anthropic tools after blacklisting company, BBC told
articles.text:
The US Department of Defence is no longer using Anthropic's AI tools, an official has told the BBC, months after it designated the company a supply chain risk on national security grounds.

The Pentagon "has ceased the use of Anthropic products", the department official said in a statement on Monday.

Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth labelled Anthropic a supply chain risk in February, and announced that the Pentagon would stop using it by late August. It is not clear why there has been a delay.

Multiple people familiar with the matter told the BBC that as recently as last week Anthopic's Claude model was still being used by the department in research, analysis and intelligence gathering as well as in military operations against Iran.

It was viewed as a critical tool for sorting through vast quantities of information, the people said. They include former US defence officials and contractors who have worked closely with the Pentagon specifically on AI.

A spokesman for Anthropic declined to comment when asked about the Pentagon's statement.

The details of the department stopping all use of Anthropic's tools have not been previously reported.

The firm had been used by the US government and military since 2024 and was the first advanced AI company to have its tools deployed in government agencies doing classified work.

But earlier this year, the Pentagon pressed it to remove its safety guardrails from Claude and give the military unfettered access to its AI products.

When Anthropic refused, citing concerns of mass surveillance and autonomous weapons, Hegseth designated the company a "national security supply-chain risk" - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US.

Anthropic said the move was "unprecedented and unlawful" and has sued the Trump administration in an effort to overturn the designation.

As this legal fight has played out in the courts, the Pentagon has signed contracts with other major tech companies, including Google, xAI and OpenAI.

OpenAI tools have been more widely adopted in recent months in some military departments, according to two people familiar with AI use in the defence department

The Pentagon's statement on Monday came in response to a question from the BBC about its use of Anthropic, after multiple people said in interviews that Claude was still being widely used.

It was embedded in a larger data platform used by the Pentagon called Maven Smart System, multiple sources said.

Maven, which is operated by Palantir, is the Pentagon's primary platform for organising intelligence and other data.

Lauren Kahn, a senior research analyst at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology said that because Claude was deeply integrated into Maven it would have been difficult to remove it quickly from the system.

"The fact that it took the Pentagon until now to remove all use of Claude from across the system is indicative that these things are not just plug and play," she said.

"Once they become integrated it can be painful to remove them," added Kahn, a former US defence official.

The BBC spoke with defence contractors who specialise in AI and have worked closely with the Pentagon, as well as former US defence officials and others familiar with the Pentagon's use of artificial intelligence. Several spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.

When Hegseth initially ordered Anthropic to be phased out of government, "there was concern with moving beyond Anthropic to OpenAI" and other tools, a former senior US defence official said.

Hegseth set a six-month deadline to phase out Anthropic on 27 February, one day before the US and Israel attacked Iran.

Pentagon employees continued to use Anthropic's Claude tools, including its powerful Mythos models, "throughout the whole period of the controversy" with the company, one of the people said.

Claude was used in particular for intelligence gathering and analysis, including through Palantir's Maven system, several sources said. Palantir, a leading defence tech firm, was founded by the billionaire ally of President Donald Trump, Peter Thiel.

articles.title: Average five-year mortgage rate hits 6% for first time in three years
articles.text:
The average interest rate on a new five-year fixed mortgage deal has hit 6% for the first time in three years, figures show.

The cost of home loans has been rising in recent weeks, as lenders face higher costs amid international concern over rising prices, interest rates, and government borrowing costs.

It means home buyers and anyone renewing a fixed deal have seen about 1,500 mortgage deals priced below 5% vanish since the start of September, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts.

It described the situation as "brutal" for borrowers, with the average rate on five-year deals now at 6%, and at 5.98% on two-year fixed mortgages.

For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage.

Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals.

Moneyfacts said that the biggest High Street lenders had made repeated fixed rate increases during September. Barclays increased selected fixed rates on four occasions, while HSBC, Lloyds Bank, Nationwide, NatWest, Santander and TSB each made three rounds of increases.

It meant that the average rate on a new five-year deal was at its highest since September 2023. On two-year deals, the average rate is at its highest since December 2023.

"Average fixed mortgage rates rising back to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers," said Rachel Springall, finance expert at Moneyfacts.

"Borrowers who were hoping mortgage rates would stabilise will be disappointed."

She said that those coming to the end of a fixed deal would be "wise to seek advice and compare deals carefully".

Some lenders could allow people to lock in a rate three months before their current deal ends, while others could allow six months, she said.

Springall said rate rises were "inevitable" because lenders' wholesale funding costs had climbed as a result of rising gilt yields.

Interest rates - known as the yield - on government bonds have been going up, meaning it costs the government more to borrow over the long term.

The knock-on impact of this on the mortgage market has meant that the number of fixed-rate deals priced below 5% has plunged by 99%, from 1,494 since the start of September 2026 to nine now.

In contrast, the number of sub-5% variable rate mortgages has remained broadly stable, Springall said, leading some borrowers to chose deals that track the Bank of England's base rate.

articles.title: Shadow chancellor vows to cut at least one tax in every Tory budget
articles.text:
Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said he hopes to scrap at least one tax every budget if the Conservatives return to power, with the so-called "mansion tax" in his sights.

Speaking at the party's conference in Birmingham, Griffith said "lower, simpler and fairer taxes" would be his "personal north star" although he noted his ambition for cuts would take place "only when we can afford to do so".

He also said he would scrap the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS), which takes effect from 2028 and introduces an extra levy for owners of properties in England valued at more than £2m.

Labour said the Tories "completely failed at every turn" to grow the economy during their 14 years in power.

Following their historic defeat in the 2024 general election, the Conservatives have been trying to rebuild and convince voters that they can be trusted again.

The Tories have faced repeated attacks from their opponents for their record in government between 2010 and 2024.

Speaking on the main stage, Griffith said: "No country in history has ever taxed its way to prosperity, so we will cut taxes, but only when we can afford to do so, and always saying clearly how we will fund that within our golden economic rule."

The party's "golden economic rule" involves at least half of all savings identified going towards "deficit reduction, with the other half going to tax cuts and pro-growth measures".

Griffith likened his approach to that of former Tory Chancellor Nigel Lawson, adding: "It's my ambition to scrap at least one tax every budget. What would we prioritise? There's a lot.

"Tax cuts that help growth, tax cuts that improve incentives to work, tax cuts that make life simpler and fairer."

The Extended Packaging Responsibility (EPR) scheme, which requires firms to cover the cost of collecting, recycling and disposing of packaging it produces, would be scrapped by the Conservatives.

Griffith sought to signal a different approach under Kemi Badenoch's leadership, telling members that the EPR was the "sort of thing the old Conservative Party went along with".

He also said Labour plans a "vindicative raid on family homes" in the form of the HVCTS, also dubbed the "mansion tax", which he would seek to scrap.

The shadow chancellor said: "It's an anti-growth tax that will distort the housing market and remove the incentive to make home improvements."

Ahead of his speech, Griffith was pressed on BBC Breakfast on whether he would keep the pensions triple lock, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham has proposed changing.

Griffith said: "We are going to keep it."

In 2021, then-backbencher Griffith wrote an article saying that the state pension triple lock was "unfair" as pensioners could "gain from the misfortune of others".

Senior Conservatives including former chancellor Jeremy Hunt and shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat have individually suggested the current triple lock is unsustainable.

articles.title: LIV Golf: Competition secures potential $300m investment to emerge from restructuring
articles.text:
LIV Golf has secured a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit in order to try to move forward with the 2027 season.

The league filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding, starting a court-supervised "restructuring process" that they hope to complete in early 2027.

It is unclear how much of the $300m LIV requires to start next year's schedule and which players will start the season.

The competition's participants are owed at least $45m (£33m) and have the option to leave.

However the agreement secures an extension for the league to discuss terms with its players, with talks now open until 25 October.

BBC Sport understands there is no obligation on players to sign on to LIV 2.0, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts with LIV Golf.

League insiders see the committed investment as a "significant" step forward in the court-supervised restructuring process.

"Our goal is to facilitate LIV Golf's emergence from the restructuring process on sound financial footing and with renewed momentum heading into the 2027 season," said Ted Goldthorpe, partner and head of BC Partners Credit, in a statement.

The credit firm, which provides financing to middle-market companies, said the funding would support the next phase of LIV Golf, under which players would become equity owners of both the league and its teams.

The financing remains subject to bankruptcy court approval and customary conditions.

"This investment is an important step forward for LIV Golf," said LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil in a statement.

"We're delivering on our major milestones, and while there is still work ahead, today marks meaningful progress toward a player-owned, team-focused, truly global league that complements the wider game and creates new opportunities for players, fans, partners, and the next generation of golfers."

Since LIV's controversial launch in 2021, more than $5bn (£3.7bn) has been spent by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), with major winners including Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau lured by lucrative contracts and vast prize money.

However, the future of the concept - and its star players - has been shrouded in uncertainty, with the 2026 season having ended early.

Documents in the petition outline money owed to LIV Golf's creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims.

Two-time major winner Rahm tops that list with an unsecured claim of $7.5m (£5.5m).

DeChambeau ($5.7m - £4.2m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m - £4.1m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m - £3.5m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m - £2.5m) are also among the top 30 creditors, as well as Brooks Koepka, who left to rejoin the PGA Tour in January but has an unsecured claim of $1.7m (£1.25m).

The total amount owed to the 14 current and former LIV players in the top 30 creditors is just over $45m (£33m).

A source familiar with the figures told BBC Sport the creditors list outlines the "amount owed and not paid for Q3" of 2026, not the full amounts.

Chapter 11 protection postpones a US company's obligations to its creditors, giving it time to reorganise its debts or sell parts of the business.

PIF is providing a bankruptcy loan of $49.6m (£36.6m) - called 'debtor in possession' (DIP) financing - to help fund the process.

articles.title: Crypto thieves attacked man in home and threatened to kill pregnant wife's baby in 'horrific' robbery
articles.text:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

A businessman was beaten with hammers by masked men who broke into his home and threatened to kill his heavily pregnant wife unless he transferred hundreds of thousands of pounds of cryptocurrency.

Speaking to the BBC, the couple, who want to remain anonymous, described the attack as "horrific" and said they feared for their unborn baby's life.

The attackers left in a car driven by a getaway driver after the man transferred his crypto savings.

Crimestoppers are offering a £10,000 reward for information in the attack, which was captured on home security footage and is being investigated by the police.

Experts say it is one of a growing type of violent theft known as a "wrench attack" targeting cryptocurrency investors.

As crypto coins have risen in value, reports of these violent robberies linked to digital assets have emerged in the UK, France and the US.

Once funds are transferred, recovering them can be extremely difficult.

The man, who the BBC is calling James, said three intruders forced their way into their Solihull home before launching an assault which lasted 45 minutes.

"The door gets pushed open, I can see gloves coming in, balaclavas," he said.

James tried to fight the men off but they hit him in the face, head and ribs with hammers.

His wife, who was seven months pregnant, was held down on the sofa by one of the criminals.

"He's got a pillow over her face," James said. "He's literally suffocating her on the sofa. I can hear her screaming, 'I can't breathe'."

The couple still had no idea what the criminals wanted until one of the men demanded James unlock his phone and hand it over.

James said the attackers appeared to know he owned cryptocurrency, but had little understanding of how to access it.

Instead, they were taking instructions from someone else connected via a live video call.

"I can hear the guy on FaceTime saying: 'Show me everything on his phone. Show me what apps he's got'," he said.

When the caller identified a crypto wallet containing substantial funds, the threats escalated dramatically.

"He was basically saying: 'Look, if you don't send us this money now, we're going to stab your wife in the stomach and kill your baby. We're going to kill your wife'," James said.

His wife, who also did not want to be named, described the attack that happened in December last year as "horrific" and said she feared James had been killed when he was unresponsive on the floor.

"It was terrifying," she said.

The woman, in her early thirties, was expecting her third child at the time and said she feared she might lose the baby due to the stress of the attack. The baby survived and was born at full term.

The men left after James transferred his savings - hundreds of thousands of pounds of cryptocurrency - to the digital wallet of the man on the video call.

They also stole several luxury Rolex watches.

James said before they left, he heard the man on the video call tell his accomplices: "You can have 10 grand each but I am taking the rest."

Unlike money held in a conventional bank account, cryptocurrency is often controlled directly by the owner through digital wallets or physical storage devices.

For criminals, that combination of speed, anonymity and irreversibility can make crypto holders attractive targets.

Whilst the vast majority of cryptocurrency theft happens online through hacks and scams, crypto investigators at Chainalysis say "wrench attacks" have surged in recent years.

According to their research, $30m (£22.6m) had been stolen so far this year up to June in violent robberies, making 2026 likely to become the single-worst year for violent crypto attacks on record. Home invasions are also on the rise this year, it found.

The US, Brazil, and Thailand are hotspots but France has seen the largest number of attacks by far, as a result of a data breach at a tax office that has apparently allowed wealthy crypto holders to be located.

"The physical security assumptions that protect traditional wealth, such as bank vaults and armored cars, do not automatically apply in crypto. Often, holders keep their assets in comparatively low security setups, like self-custody wallets, that can be compromised without any institutional gatekeeper standing in the way," said researchers in their report.

James said he became an amateur investor in crypto coins in 2020 and made enough money to quit his job in 2023 to trade full time.

Now he has lost everything and is looking to get back to his traditional job.

Police have yet to identify the attackers.

Crimestoppers is offering a £10,000 reward for information leading to progress in the investigation.

Alan Edwards from the charity hopes people might have information about the three attackers, the driver who was parked outside without a face covering, or the man on the phone.

"These criminals are obviously serious and part of some kind of organised crime gang," he said.

"People might be scared to give us information but we are independent of the police and keep people completely anonymous."

The three attackers are all thought to be in their late teens or early 20s and one of them was a black male with a scar under his left eyebrow.

James said he has little hope of recovering the stolen funds, but instead wanted to see those responsible brought to justice.

He also wants his experience to serve as a warning.

"They threatened my wife and my baby," he said. "People need to understand these risks are real."

articles.title: US supreme court hears big oil’s bid to block climate damage lawsuits
articles.text:
The US supreme court began its new nine-month term hearing arguments on Monday in a major case in which big oil companies attempted to strike a fatal blow against lawsuits that seek to hold them accountable for the climate crisis.

After the almost two-hour hearing, while it was not yet clear which way the justices were leaning, experts said the court may find it challenging to write a majority decision siding with industry.

In Suncor Energy Inc v County Commissioners of Boulder County, local officials in Boulder are suing Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil in state court to force the companies to share a portion of the costs that the climate crisis has imposed on local taxpayers. However, Exxon and Canada-based Suncor are arguing that federal law prevents state courts from hearing Boulder’s climate change lawsuit.

If the supreme court justices side with Boulder or decide that the case is not in their jurisdiction, then it would continue in state court. But if the fossil fuel industry convinces the justices, the decision could apply not only to the Boulder case, but also to dozens of other climate cases brought by state and local governments around the US.

As a result of Justice Samuel Alito’s recusal from the case, there are only five conservative justices weighing in, so Boulder county must only convince one conservative justice to win, assuming the three liberal justices back Boulder. Some noted that the justices focused their questions primarily on the merits of the case rather than asking if the court had jurisdiction to hear it, suggesting they will make a decision on the question of whether federal law pre-empts Boulder’s state climate case.

Kannon Shanmugam, a lawyer for the fossil fuel companies, told the justices that climate change was a pressing issue, but state cases such as the one filed by Boulder were the wrong way to resolve it, and the issue should be left to lawmakers. He argued that if the cases were heard in state courts, it would allow a high number of lawsuits to be filed. “The breadth of Boulder’s argument is astonishing,” he said.

Shanmugam argued that climate change is different from other interstate pollution cases “because the claim runs through global climate change” and involves anyone who uses fossil fuels worldwide.

Kirti Datla, the director of Earthjustice’s strategic legal advocacy program, said the industry lawyer needed five justices to agree with him. “Some of the justices seemed to be persuaded by the idea that climate change is different, or the sheer number of these suits creates a problem of a different kind,” Datla said. But she added that the justices were struggling to come up with reasons based in law that would support the industry arguments. “It’s always been Suncor’s task to provide them with clear answers to those questions, and I didn’t hear clear answers to those questions in argument.”

Dennis Fan, the founder and director of the Appellate Litigation Clinic at Columbia Law School who wrote an amicus brief in the case, said it was too close to call, but he was concerned for the future of the climate cases. “They focused more on the merits,” he said. “That had me much more worried for Boulder.”

Fan said the industry hopes this case is going to be the “death blow” to this type of lawsuit. “The industry is going for the home run … They’re thinking, ‘If we win this argument, there will never, ever be climate change litigation again.’”

Boulder officials filed a lawsuit in Colorado court in 2018 arguing that Exxon and Suncor concealed and misrepresented to the public what they knew about the damage that burning fossil fuels would do to the climate, and that they should pay for the resulting costs of disasters. Initially, the firms sought to have the case moved to federal court. Then when the Colorado supreme court allowed Boulder’s case to make its way toward trial in state court, Exxon and Suncor appealed that ruling up to the supreme court, arguing it should be dismissed on grounds of federal pre-emption.

Typically, cases must be decided by lower courts before reaching the supreme court, but the justices agreed to hear this case while the state case is ongoing. “That’s an incredibly weird thing to have happen,” Fan said.

The supreme court considered whether it had proper jurisdiction to hear Boulder’s case right now, and whether federal law pre-empted Boulder’s case from being heard in state court.

Congress has the power to pass federal laws that invalidate state laws, but the question is whether there are any federal laws that invalidate state climate cases. “They’ve had a little bit of difficulty identifying exactly what that source of federal law is,” Fan said. For instance, the fossil fuel companies claim that the federal Clean Air Act pre-empts Boulder’s case from state court, even though the law specifies that “air pollution control at its source is the primary responsibility of states and local governments”.

So the fossil fuel companies in their brief claimed that supreme court decisions from a century ago suggested that federal courts have power to hear environmental cases, even without federal laws on the books, and that these decisions created a “federal common law” governing environmental lawsuits across state lines. They asserted that this federal common law was still in effect and existed in the “structure of the Constitution” even though the federal Clean Air Act has since declared states have primary jurisdiction over local air pollution.

Shanmugam presented the constitutional theory to the justices on Monday, but Kevin Russell, Boulder’s attorney, repeatedly drew their attention back to the constitution. Russell argued that the industry attorney was asking them to “jump through a number of hoops” to answer a complicated question. “Instead, I would suggest that the court can and should directly answer the question: what in the constitution implicitly prohibits Colorado or any other state’s law from applying to these claims?”

Datla of Earthjustice said some conservative justices appeared to agree with Boulder on this point. “Chief Justice [John Roberts] and Justice [Neil] Gorsuch seemed to ask questions that indicated that they thought that broad constitutional rule was complicated at a minimum,” she said.

Datla said the reaction of the conservative justices suggested they would find it difficult to write a decision supporting Suncor. “The fact that there wasn’t a clear position that the conservative justices seem to coalesce around as to which one of Suncor’s arguments was right is, I think, telling that maybe they don’t all think this is a foregone conclusion.”

The supreme court has not historically agreed with the argument the oil companies are making, Fan said. He pointed to the tobacco and opioid companies that previously faced state public nuisance cases. “For decades, the tobacco industry tried to get the supreme court and other courts to stop state court litigation from happening against the tobacco industry, and they failed every single time,” he said.

Climate advocates and wildfire survivors rallied on Monday morning outside the supreme court in Washington DC.

Daryl McCool, an artist who lost her home when the 2021 Marshall fire destroyed her neighborhood in Boulder county, Colorado, is not involved in the case but planned to attend the rally. The fire caused damage estimated at more than $2bn, and a recent report estimated that the climate crisis could cost Colorado up to $37bn by 2050. “The case itself is meaningful because it affects every single human, every single creature, it affects everyone that is on this earth,” McCool said.

The Trump administration has sided with the oil companies and has carried out a series of pollution regulations, including revoking the 2009 bedrock scientific determination that gives the government the ability to regulate climate-heating pollution.

A ruling is expected next summer.

articles.title: Mark Thompson will remain chief executive at CNN after Paramount sale
articles.text:
Mark Thompson, who since 2023 has served as chair and chief executive of CNN after a storied career in British and American media, will retain his role even after Paramount Skydance takes control of the company, he announced in a memo to network staffers on Monday morning.

While Thompson wrote that the “specifics of how CNN will plug into and operate in the new company have yet to be finalized”, he offered some pledges about his role at the combined company, which will be led by David Ellison, the Paramount Skydance chief executive, after the company merges with CNN parent company Warner Bros Discovery. The deal is expected to formally close on Tuesday.

“First, I’m convinced that from David Ellison on down, Paramount Skydance leadership really does believe in news alongside entertainment as a top strategic opportunity for our new company,” Thompson wrote. “They’ve seen our digital strategy and are as excited about it as we are.

“And second, having now spoken to them at length on the topic, I have real confidence that they both understand and will fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for. That’s why I will be leading CNN into this new chapter as it becomes one of Skydance’s suite of major media assets and global brands, and leading it as an independent editor-in-chief with the same responsibilities and prerogatives that I have now.”

The decision by Paramount Skydance leadership will bring relief to many CNN employees who feared a complete overhaul of the network. Some employees had also shared concerns that Ellison could install Bari Weiss, editor in chief of CBS News, atop the cable news network. (The Wall Street Journal first reported that Ellison had asked Thompson to stay on.)

“That sound you hear is a giant sigh of relief from halls of Techwood,” said a CNN producer, who was not authorized to comment, referring to the company’s Atlanta headquarters. That sentiment was shared by other CNN employees who spoke with the Guardian.

According to an announcement of the combined company’s leadership team, Weiss will also remain in her role as editor in chief of CBS News, despite some speculation about a potential change in her purview.

Thompson, 69, was brought on to take charge of CNN in 2023 after the tumultuous leadership of chief executive Chris Licht, who lacked network management experience and lasted just over a year. Thompson had previously served as director-general of the BBC from 2004 to 2012 and then as president and CEO of the New York Times from 2012 to 2020.

At CNN, Thompson has prioritized the network’s digital and streaming operations, as well as the creation of a new direct-to-consumer product called CNN All Access in October 2025. The CNN producer credited Thompson with “stabilizing” the business and helping to build its post-linear television future.

Thompson has also had his hands full with Donald Trump’s White House, which last month barred CNN – along with MS Now and Politico – from the building before a judge temporarily restored access.

A former longtime CNN producer said that Thompson’s presence would be reassuring because he is a known entity. “They know what he brings,” the person said.

When Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of CNN parent company Warner Bros Discovery closes on Tuesday, after the settlement of lawsuits aimed at blocking the deal, the company will begin the process of integrating the various media assets it has acquired.

It is unclear if, when or how CNN and CBS News will be merged, though they will share a parent company. The two networks have different corporate structures and serve different audiences. At an industry conference on 30 September, Paramount’s chief legal officer, Makan Delrahim, noted those distinctions. “CBS News is a handful of hours of programming,” he reportedly said. “CNN is 24-7. Just completely different markets.”

While both CBS News and CNN have large American audiences, CNN has a much larger international footprint, and there has been speculation that its foreign team could take precedence if the companies are merged. There is also the expectation of widespread layoffs across the entire company, including at CBS News and CNN, as part of an effort to slash costs.

And there have been concerns about whether the Ellison family, which controls a large chunk of American media and entertainment assets, could move CNN in a more conservative direction, a fear that Ellison himself has dismissed.

As part of a settlement reached between Paramount and a coalition of 12 state attorneys general last month who sued to block the deal, the company has agreed to create a five-person news editorial independence board within 180 days of closing the deal. The board will “establish guiding editorial and journalism principles for the combined entity’s news channels” and will ensure those principles are adhered to. But some employees at CNN and CBS News have dismissed the planned board, fearing it will lack teeth.

Thompson hinted at the uncertainty surrounding the merger in his memo. “I know many of you have had trepidations about this moment. That’s understandable – indeed, as I’ve hinted before, I’ve had the odd moment or two myself!” he said. “But I want to say that on the eve of the acquisition of CNN by Paramount Skydance, I find myself in a very positive frame of mind. I really do believe we’ll be working alongside a team who don’t just have real vision and real energy, but real values as well.”

Thompson told CNN employees that he would have more details to share on Tuesday.

articles.title: Manchester City: Rival clubs want more than relegation from the Premier League
articles.text:
A number of Premier League clubs want Manchester City to be hit with both "retrospective punishments" and sanctions for the future for their mass financial rule-breaking, sources have told BBC Sport.

An independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

City have appealed against the verdict.

However, there is said to be a consensus among a group of top-flight club executives that if City's appeal is unsuccessful, the sanctions should make reparations for the period when they broke the rules, while also limiting their powers in future.

There is also a feeling from at least four Premier League boardrooms that a "one-hit" points deduction resulting in relegation to the Championship would be an insufficient punishment given the severity of City's wrongdoing.

There is understood to be nuance in exactly what clubs consider a fitting penalty for the eight-time Premier League champions, who were found guilty of all serious financial rule breaches in a damning verdict by an independent commission.

One senior club source said City should be stripped of their titles, and added there was "no great rush" among clubs to push for the redistribution of trophies, but rather to take honours away and leave them vacant.

The source warned the credibility of the Premier League would be lost if City were allowed to keep the eight major trophies they won during the period they have been found guilty.

However, in a sign of a range of opinions across the league, BBC Sport was previously told there was little appetite among other clubs for City to be stripped of titles.

Regarding the timescale for sanctions in the future, there is a concern among club executives that a sanction applied just to one season would merely provide City with a "bump in the road" given the likelihood of them returning to the Premier League at the first time of asking.

A number of Premier League figures therefore believe any points deduction should be split over multiple seasons, while there is also a sense that transfer bans that stretch over a number of windows would also significantly hinder City's ability to regain their top-flight status as quickly as possible.

One club source also said it would be "bizarre, almost obtuse" if City were able to trade in the upcoming January transfer window, if this process is ongoing and sanctions have not been applied.

Some clubs cited feeling "in the dark" regards the Premier League, including around the chronology and timescales of the appeal and the sanctions hearing.

However, sources said there was "empathy" and "understanding" about the difficult position the Premier League is in, given the gravity of this situation and the ongoing legal process.

Regarding financial reparations, one idea that has been mooted - and which a club source found "merit" in - was to apply a "tariff-based system", whereby City's past league finishing positions would be altered via a points deduction.

Rival clubs could then be paid compensation by City based on where they would have finished versus where they did finish.

BBC Sport understands Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca will speak to players collectively after they arrive back from international duty on Thursday, before their Premier League match against Liverpool on Sunday (16:30 BST).

The trip to Anfield is their first game since news of the verdict broke.

Merseyside Police says it has received queries in relation to the match, and when asked by BBC Sport if any special measures would be put in place the force said it will have "an appropriate policing operation in place on the day".

Sources at Liverpool have told BBC Sport it is a case of "business as usual" and there are no extra measures being put in place. Conversations and meetings between the club, supporters and relevant authorities take place before every home game.

One source said while everyone "has the right to express their feelings" they hoped supporters would not overstep the mark.
